method_card.title: Two-Way Tables, Tree Diagrams and Venn Diagrams
method_card.content:
Three visual tools help you organise probability problems with two or three events.

A two-way table shows frequencies for two categorical variables. To find a probability, divide the relevant cell count by the total.

A tree diagram shows sequential events. Each branch carries a probability; multiply along a branch to find the probability of that path: $$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B | A)$$

Add the probabilities of separate branches that give the same outcome. For independent events, \(P(B|A) = P(B)\), so the second-branch probabilities stay the same regardless of the first outcome. For sampling without replacement, the denominators on the second level change — this is the most common error.

A Venn diagram places outcomes in overlapping circles. The region inside both circles is \(A \cap B\) (A and B). The outside region is neither A nor B. Total all regions to find the denominator for a probability.

Higher tier only — conditional probability notation: $$P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$$ This formula will be given in the question. \(P(A|B)\) means “the probability of A given that B has already occurred.”
steps: Identify how many events are involved and whether they are sequential (tree) or categorical (two-way/Venn)
For tree diagrams: write probabilities on each branch, then multiply along each path
Adjust second-branch denominators if the problem says 'without replacement'
Add path probabilities if the question asks for outcomes that can happen in more than one way
For Venn diagrams: fill in the intersection first, then work outwards to each circle, then outside
For conditional probability (Higher): divide P(A and B) by P(B)

exam_context.marks: 3 to 6 marks; tree diagram questions often include a 2-mark structured calculation followed by a 2-mark interpretation or without-replacement extension
exam_context.frequency: Tree diagrams and two-way tables appear on nearly every paper; Venn diagrams appear regularly; conditional probability notation is tested at Higher tier

worked_examples.question: A two-way table shows sports preferences for 50 students. Boys: 12 prefer football, 8 prefer swimming. Girls: 15 prefer football, 15 prefer swimming. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability the student prefers swimming?

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the total who prefer swimming
steps.content: Boys who prefer swimming = 8. Girls who prefer swimming = 15. Total = 8 + 15 = 23.

worked_examples.question: A bag contains 5 red counters and 3 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Using the tree diagram values below, find the probability that both counters are the same colour. First draw — P(red) = 5/8, P(blue) = 3/8. If red first: P(red second) = 4/7, P(blue second) = 3/7. If blue first: P(red second) = 5/7, P(blue second) = 2/7.

A Venn diagram has two circles, A and B, inside a rectangle. The values are: only A = 7, A and B (intersection) = 4, only B = 9, neither = 5. A student is chosen at random from all 25 people. Given that the student is in set B, what is the probability they are also in set A? (Higher: use the conditional probability formula P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B), which is given.)

steps.label: Step 1 — Find P(A and B)
steps.content: Number in A and B = 4. Total = 25. \(P(A \text{ and } B) = \frac{4}{25}\)

bronze.display: A two-way table shows data about 60 students. Studying maths: 18 male, 14 female. Not studying maths: 12 male, 16 female. A student is picked at random. What is the probability the student is female?
A tree diagram shows two coin flips. Each branch shows P(heads) = 1/2 and P(tails) = 1/2. What is P(heads then tails)?
A Venn diagram has two circles P and Q. Only P = 6, P and Q intersection = 3, only Q = 9, neither = 2. How many people are in the diagram altogether?

misconceptions.message: Total = only P + intersection + only Q + neither = 6 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 20.

bronze.display: In a class of 30 students, 18 study French, 12 study Spanish, and 5 study both. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability the student studies French but not Spanish?
A tree diagram shows P(win) = 0.6 and P(lose) = 0.4 for Game 1. P(win) = 0.7 and P(lose) = 0.3 for Game 2 (independent). What is P(win both games)?

misconceptions.message: P(win both) = 0.6 x 0.7 = 0.42. Multiply along the 'win-win' branch.

bronze.display: A two-way table shows transport preferences. Boys: 10 bus, 8 cycle. Girls: 12 bus, 10 cycle. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability the student cycles?
From a Venn diagram: circle A only = 5, A and B intersection = 3, B only = 7, neither = 4. A person is chosen at random. What is the probability they are in A or B (or both)?
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. One ball is drawn and replaced, then a second is drawn. What is the probability both are red?

misconceptions.message: P(red) = 4/10 on each draw (with replacement). P(red and red) = 4/10 x 4/10 = 16/100 = 4/25.

silver.display: A bag contains 7 red counters and 3 green counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Using these probabilities: P(red 1st) = 7/10; if red 1st then P(red 2nd) = 6/9, P(green 2nd) = 3/9; if green 1st then P(red 2nd) = 7/9, P(green 2nd) = 2/9. Find P(at least one green).

misconceptions.message: P(red, red) = 7/10 x 6/9 = 42/90. P(at least one green) = 1 - 42/90 = 48/90 = 8/15. Or add the three non-red-red paths. Make sure denominators change on second draw.

silver.display: A two-way table shows 100 people surveyed about exercise and diet. Good diet + exercises: 35. Good diet + does not exercise: 20. Poor diet + exercises: 15. Poor diet + does not exercise: 30. What is the probability a randomly chosen person has a good diet given that they exercise?

misconceptions.message: Total who exercise = 35 + 15 = 50. Of those, 35 have a good diet. P(good diet | exercises) = 35/50 = 7/10.

silver.display: Two events A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(A and B)?

misconceptions.message: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) = 0.4 x 0.3 = 0.12.

silver.display: A fair spinner has sections 1–5. It is spun twice. What is the probability of getting an odd number both times? (Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5.)

misconceptions.message: P(odd) = 3/5 on each spin. Spins are independent. P(odd and odd) = 3/5 x 3/5 = 9/25.

silver.display: In a Venn diagram for 40 people: A only = 12, A and B = 8, B only = 10, neither = 10. A person is chosen at random. What is P(A)?

misconceptions.message: P(A) includes people in A only AND the intersection: (12 + 8) / 40 = 20/40 = 1/2. Do not forget the intersection region.

silver.display: A box has 3 defective and 7 working light bulbs. Two bulbs are tested without replacement. What is the probability that exactly one is defective? Use these branch values: P(def 1st) = 3/10; if def 1st: P(working 2nd) = 7/9; if working 1st: P(def 2nd) = 3/9.

misconceptions.message: P(def then working) = 3/10 x 7/9 = 21/90. P(working then def) = 7/10 x 3/9 = 21/90. Add: 42/90 = 7/15. There are two ways to get exactly one defective.

gold.display: From a Venn diagram for 60 students: only hobby A = 18, A and B intersection = 6, only hobby B = 14, neither = 22. Using the conditional probability formula P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B), find P(A|B). Give your answer as a fraction. (This formula will be given in the exam.)
A bag has 4 red and 5 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. Find P(second is red | first was blue). Use these values: if blue first, P(red second) = 4/8. Give your answer as a fraction.

misconceptions.message: After drawing one blue, 8 counters remain: 4 red and 4 blue. P(red 2nd | blue 1st) = 4/8 = 1/2. The denominator must decrease because a counter has been removed.

gold.display: Events A and B: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent? Select the correct justification.
options: Yes — P(A) x P(B) = 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.2 = P(A and B), so A and B are independent
No — P(A and B) should equal P(A) + P(B) for independent events
Yes — because P(A and B) is not zero

misconceptions.message: The test for independence is P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Here 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.2, which matches P(A and B) = 0.2. So A and B are independent.

gold.display: Two cards are drawn from a standard 52-card pack without replacement. Using P(heart 1st) = 13/52, P(heart 2nd | heart 1st) = 12/51, P(heart 2nd | not heart 1st) = 13/51 — find P(exactly one heart). Give your answer as a fraction.

A survey of 80 adults asks whether they own a pet (P) and whether they exercise daily (E). P only = 22, P and E = 10, E only = 28, neither = 20. Using P(P|E) = P(P and E) / P(E), find P(P|E) as a fraction. (Formula given.)

prerequisites.title: Relative Risk, Absolute Risk and Risk Communication
